usage: 기쁨 ends in a vowel, so the subject marker is 이, not 가
the fixed verb for emotions is 느끼다 'feel', not 가지다 'have'
Koreans 'divide' (나누다) a feeling rather than 'share' it the English way
큰 'big' is the natural adjective for 기쁨, not 높은 'high'
examples: 참 기뻐요
I'm really glad
the everyday way to express the feeling is the adjective 기쁘다, not the noun 기쁨
합격 소식에 큰 기쁨을 느꼈어요
I felt great joy at the news that I passed
에 marks the trigger of the emotion, like 'at' the news
아이의 웃음이 부모에게는 가장 큰 기쁨이에요
A child's laughter is the greatest joy to parents
에게는 marks the experiencer; this is a heartfelt, almost written register
nuance: 기쁨 is the noun 'joy/gladness', the nominalized form of the adjective 기쁘다 (기쁘 + ㅁ). It names a bright, often momentary delight sparked by a specific good event — passing an exam, a reunion, good news. The near-synonym to separate is 행복 (幸福), 'happiness': 행복 is a broad, lasting state of life ('a happy marriage'), while 기쁨 is the sharp spike of gladness at one happy thing. So you feel 기쁨 about your friend's wedding but wish them lifelong 행복. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the noun in speech: to say 'I'm happy/glad' a Korean almost always uses the adjective 기뻐요, and saves the noun 기쁨 for when it is the subject or object of a sentence (기쁨을 느끼다, 기쁨이 크다). Note too that the verb is 느끼다 'feel', never 가지다 'have'.

usage: 슬픔 + 이; 밀려오다 'surge in' is the vivid collocation for waves of feeling
느끼다 'feel' is the fixed verb, not 있다 'have/exist'
슬픔 collocates with 깊은 'deep', mirroring English
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is an idiom for being lost in an emotion
examples: 너무 슬퍼요
I'm so sad
to say you feel sad, use the adjective 슬프다, not the noun
반려동물이 떠나서 큰 슬픔을 느꼈어요
I felt great sadness because my pet passed away
-아서/어서 gives the cause; 떠나다 'leave' is a gentle euphemism for death
그 영화는 잔잔한 슬픔을 남겼어요
That film left a quiet sadness
잔잔한 'calm, gentle' + 슬픔 captures a lingering, bittersweet mood
nuance: 슬픔 is the noun 'sadness/sorrow', built from the adjective 슬프다 (슬프 + ㅁ). It is a heavy, quiet grief that wells up inside — from loss, parting, or disappointment — and it lingers, unlike a flash of irritation. Compare it with 우울 (憂鬱), 'depression/gloom': 우울 is a duller, more clinical low mood with no single cause ('I feel 우울 today for no reason'), whereas 슬픔 is sorrow you can usually point to a reason for. It also differs from 아쉬움, the mild 'too bad / wish it were otherwise' regret. The classic English-speaker mistake is using the noun where the adjective belongs: 'I am sad' is 슬퍼요 (adjective), never 슬픔이에요, which would mean 'It is sadness'. Reserve the noun 슬픔 for subject/object roles (슬픔을 느끼다, 슬픔이 깊다).

usage: 분노 + 가; 치밀다 'boil/well up' is the set verb for rising rage
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb for the emotion
참다 'endure/suppress' is the habitual partner for restraining 분노
분노 + 의 + noun links the feeling to what shows it
examples: 너무 화가 나요
I'm so angry
in daily speech the everyday phrase is 화가 나다, not the heavy noun 분노
불공정한 판정에 분노를 느꼈어요
I felt anger at the unfair ruling
에 marks the trigger; 분노 suits weighty, public injustices
시민들의 분노가 거리로 터져 나왔어요
The citizens' anger burst out into the streets
this grave, news-style register is exactly where 분노 belongs
nuance: 분노 is the Sino-Korean noun for 'anger/wrath', 분노 憤怒 — 憤 'indignation' + 怒 'rage' — so by its very characters it is righteous, intense fury, not petty annoyance. The crucial contrast for learners is the everyday word 화 (火, literally 'fire'): in conversation Koreans say 화가 나다 'anger arises' or 화를 내다 'show anger' for ordinary irritation, while 분노 is reserved for grave, often moral or collective rage — social injustice, betrayal, public outrage — and shows up in news, speeches, and writing far more than in casual chat. Saying 분노했어요 over a late bus sounds comically overblown; 짜증 났어요 'I got annoyed' or 화가 났어요 fits. The pitfall: English 'angry' is one word covering all intensities, so learners overuse 분노. Match the register — keep 분노 for the heavy stuff and use 화/짜증 for daily friction.

Mismatched verb: 분노를 하다 is wrong. Use 분노를 느끼다 'feel anger', 분노가 치밀다 'anger surges', or 분노하다 as one verb.

usage: 두려움 + 이; 밀려오다 conveys fear creeping or surging in
느끼다 'feel' is the standard verb for this inner emotion
이겨내다 'win out over' is the inspiring partner verb
noun + 없이 'without' is the set adverbial phrase
examples: 혼자 자는 게 무서워요
I'm scared to sleep alone
for plain 'I'm scared' use the adjective 무섭다, not the noun 두려움
새 도전 앞에서 두려움을 느꼈어요
I felt fear before a new challenge
앞에서 'in front of' frames what you face; 두려움 fits abstract dread
실패에 대한 두려움이 그를 멈추게 했어요
Fear of failure made him stop
N에 대한 두려움 'fear of/about N' is the standard frame for what is feared
nuance: 두려움 is the noun 'fear/dread', from the adjective 두렵다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 두렵 + 음 → 두려움). It names a deep, often anticipatory inner fear — of the future, failure, the unknown — more reflective and lasting than a sudden jolt. Separate two relatives: 무서움/무섭다 is concrete, gut-level scared ('a scary movie', 'the dog is scary'), the word you actually say in conversation, whereas 두려움 is heavier, more abstract and literary, and is the one paired with big life anxieties. A third, 공포 (恐怖), is sheer terror/horror, the genre word for horror films and panic. So a spider triggers 무서움, an uncertain future triggers 두려움, a horror movie deals in 공포. The English-speaker pitfall: 'fear' maps to all of these, so beginners overuse 두려움 in casual speech where 무서워요 is natural, and forget the ㅂ-irregular spelling (두렵다 → 두려워요, 두려움).

usage: 외로움을 타다 'catch/feel loneliness' is the idiomatic set phrase, like catching a chill
외로움 pairs with 깊은 'deep', as in English
달래다 'comfort/soothe' is the tender partner verb
examples: 요즘 좀 외로워요
I'm a bit lonely these days
for 'I feel lonely' use the adjective 외롭다, not the noun
객지 생활에서 외로움을 느껴요
I feel loneliness living away from home
에서 marks the situation that produces the feeling
사람들 속에서도 외로움을 느낄 때가 있어요
There are times I feel lonely even amid people
속에서도 'even within' captures the ache of loneliness in a crowd
nuance: 외로움 is the noun 'loneliness', from the adjective 외롭다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 외롭 + 음 → 외로움). It is the empty, aching emotional sense of being cut off from others — a feeling you can have even surrounded by people. The sharp contrast learners need is 혼자 'alone' (just the physical fact of being by oneself, no feeling implied) versus 외로움 (the emotion). You can be 혼자 and perfectly content, or in a crowd and full of 외로움. A subtler neighbor is 고독 (孤獨), 'solitude': 고독 is weightier, often chosen or even noble — the solitude of an artist — while 외로움 is the plain, sad pang of missing connection. A very Korean collocation is 외로움을 타다, literally 'to ride/catch loneliness', meaning someone gets lonely easily. Pitfall: don't equate 외로움 with 혼자 — being alone and feeling lonely are different words, and 'I'm lonely' is the adjective 외로워요, not 외로움이에요.

usage: 그리움 + 이; 사무치다 'pierce to the bone' is the literary set verb
에 젖다 'be soaked in' is the poetic idiom for being filled with the feeling
그리움 + 의 + noun marks who/what is missed
examples: 엄마가 보고 싶어요
I miss my mom
to say 'I miss ___' Koreans use 보고 싶다 'want to see', not the noun 그리움
고향에 대한 그리움이 밀려와요
Longing for my hometown washes over me
N에 대한 그리움 'longing for N' is the standard frame
오래된 편지가 그 시절의 그리움을 불러일으켜요
An old letter stirs up longing for those days
불러일으키다 'stir up/evoke' pairs with deep nostalgic feelings
nuance: 그리움 is the noun 'longing/yearning', from the verb 그리워하다 / adjective 그립다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 그립 + 음 → 그리움). It is a warm, bittersweet ache for someone or somewhere absent — a person far away, a lost time, your hometown — blending sweetness with quiet sorrow, close to English 'nostalgia' when aimed at the past. The key contrast is the everyday verb 보고 싶다, literally 'want to see', which is how Koreans actually say 'I miss you/it' in conversation; 그리움 is the noun naming that emotion and lands more poetic and reflective, common in songs and writing. Don't confuse it with 후회 'regret' (wishing you'd acted differently) — 그리움 carries no fault, only tender missing. The pitfall for English speakers: 'I miss you' is not 당신의 그리움 or 그리움이에요; it is 보고 싶어요. Save the noun 그리움 for when the feeling itself is the subject or object (그리움이 밀려오다, 그리움을 느끼다), and remember the ㅂ-irregular: 그립다 → 그리워요, 그리움.

usage: 즐거움 + 이; 가득하다 'be full' collocates with abundant feeling
누리다 'enjoy, partake of' is the elevated partner verb for pleasures one gets to have
소소한 'small, modest' + 즐거움 is a very common warm collocation
examples: 오늘 정말 즐거웠어요
I really had fun today
for 'it was fun / I had fun' use the adjective 즐겁다, not the noun
여행에서 큰 즐거움을 느꼈어요
I felt great enjoyment on the trip
에서 marks the activity that gives the pleasure
요리는 저에게 소소한 즐거움 중 하나예요

Draw the line clearly: 기쁨 spikes at a good event (you passed!), while 즐거움 flows from an enjoyable experience (the party was fun). The everyday word is the adjective 재미있다 'be fun/interesting', used for movies, games, and stories; 즐겁다/즐거움 is a touch warmer and more about your own good time than about the thing being amusing. A lovely set phrase is 소소한 즐거움 'small everyday pleasures'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'fun' is an adjective in English, so learners say 즐거움이에요 meaning 'it's fun' — but that's the noun ('It is enjoyment'); say 즐거워요 or 재미있어요. Mind the ㅂ-irregular: 즐겁다 → 즐거워요, 즐거움.

부끄러움이 많다 'have much shyness' describes a bashful personality
도 없이 'without even' intensifies the absence of embarrassment

I was so embarrassed when presenting
for 'I felt shy/embarrassed' use the adjective 부끄럽다
칭찬을 받고 부끄러움을 느꼈어요

nuance: 부끄러움 is the noun 'shyness/embarrassment', from the adjective 부끄럽다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽 + 음 → 부끄러움). Crucially, contrast it with 창피함/창피하다, which is sharper, more 'mortified / lost face' embarrassment — tripping in public, an awkward gaffe you cringe at — and with 수치심 (羞恥心), a heavy, dignity-wounding shame tied to disgrace. So a blush at a compliment is 부끄러움, spilling coffee on yourself in front of everyone leans 창피함, and a scandal that destroys your honor is 수치심. A native collocation is 부끄러움을 타다 'to be the shy type', parallel to 외로움을 타다. The pitfall: English 'shame/embarrassed' lumps these together, so learners use 부끄러움 for grave moral shame, where 수치심 is correct, or for sharp public mortification, where 창피하다 fits better. And as always, 'I'm embarrassed' is 부끄러워요 (adjective), not 부끄러움이에요. Watch the ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽다 → 부끄러워요.

usage: 용기 ends in a vowel → 가; 필요하다 'be needed' is the set partner
용기를 내다 'put out courage' is the fixed idiom — not 만들다 'make' or 가지다 'have'
잃다 'lose' is the opposing partner verb
북돋우다 'spur on' is the verb for giving others courage
examples: 용기를 내세요
Be brave / Take heart
용기를 내다 is THE everyday phrase for 'work up the nerve'
고백할 용기를 냈어요
I worked up the courage to confess
Verb-ㄹ/을 용기 'the courage to do' modifies 용기 with what you dared
응원해 주셔서 용기를 얻었어요
Your support gave me courage
용기를 얻다 'gain courage' pairs naturally with encouragement from others
nuance: 용기 is the Sino-Korean noun 'courage/bravery', 용기 勇氣 — 勇 'brave' + 氣 'spirit/energy' — literally 'brave spirit'. It is the positive inner strength to face fear or do something hard, a trait Koreans openly praise. The most important thing to learn is its fixed collocation: courage is something you 내다 'put out / produce', so 'work up the courage' is 용기를 내다, and the everyday imperative 용기를 내세요 means 'be brave / take heart' — using 가지다 'have' or 만들다 'make' here sounds wrong. Contrast 용기 with 자신감 (自信感) 'confidence/self-assurance': 자신감 is belief in your own ability ('confidence in your English'), built from skill, while 용기 is the nerve to act despite fear, regardless of skill. You also 얻다 'gain' or 잃다 'lose' 용기. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — saying 용기를 가지다 instead of the idiomatic 용기를 내다 — and conflating 'courage' with 'confidence' (자신감), which are distinct in Korean.

usage: 희망 + 이; 있다/없다 'there is/isn't' is the core partner
unlike most feelings, 희망 naturally takes 가지다 'have', plus 품다 'cherish'
잃다 'lose' is the standard opposite collocation
희망 + 의 + noun forms set phrases like 희망의 끈 'a thread of hope'
examples: 아직 희망이 있어요
There's still hope
있다 'exist' is the everyday verb; 아직 'still' is a frequent companion
미래에 대한 희망을 가지고 있어요
I hold hope for the future
N에 대한 희망 'hope for/about N' is the standard frame for what is hoped for
작은 희망의 끈을 놓지 마세요
Don't let go of that small thread of hope
희망의 끈 'thread of hope' + 놓다 'let go' is a set encouraging idiom
nuance: 희망 is the Sino-Korean noun 'hope', 희망 希望 — 希 'wish/hope for' + 望 'gaze into the distance, aspire' — so its very characters paint hope as gazing toward something wished for. It is a bright, forward-looking expectation that good things will come, weightier and more enduring than a casual wish, and it gives comfort and strength in hard times. Separate it from two relatives. 소원 (所願) is a specific 'wish' you make — the one wish on a shooting star or a birthday candle — concrete and singular, whereas 희망 is broader, an outlook on the future. 기대 (期待) is 'expectation/anticipation', leaning toward something you fairly confidently await ('I have high 기대 for the movie'), while 희망 keeps the sense of hoping for an uncertain but desired outcome. A notable point of grammar: although feelings usually take 느끼다, 희망 prefers 가지다 'have', 품다 'cherish', or 있다/없다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 희망 for a small, immediate wish where 소원 or the grammar pattern -았으면 좋겠다 'I wish that…' is natural, e.g. for 'I hope it doesn't rain' Koreans say 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요, not a sentence built on 희망.

usage: 추억 + 이; 떠오르다 'float up' is the set verb for memories surfacing
추억을 만들다 'make memories' is the exact, very common collocation
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is the idiom for reminiscing
추억 + 의 + noun marks a spot tied to fond recollection
examples: 좋은 추억이 많아요
I have many good memories
추억 collocates with 좋은 'good' and 많다 'be many'
같이 여행하면서 추억을 많이 만들었어요
We made many memories traveling together
추억을 만들다 'make memories' — the natural verb is 만들다, never 하다
이 노래를 들으면 학창 시절 추억에 잠겨요
When I hear this song I sink into memories of my school days
추억에 잠기다 captures dwelling in fond nostalgia
nuance: 추억 is the Sino-Korean noun for a 'cherished memory', 추억 追憶 — 追 'pursue, trace back' + 憶 'recollect' — so literally 'tracing back a recollection', a warm act of looking fondly on the past. The vital contrast is with 기억 (記憶), 'memory' in the neutral, factual sense: 기억 is your mental record of any information — a phone number, where you parked, what someone said — and can be good or bad, while 추억 is specifically a treasured, emotionally warm past experience you reminisce about. So you 기억하다 'remember' a fact, but you 추억을 만들다 'make memories' on a trip and look back on 좋은 추억 'good memories' from childhood. A signature collocation is 추억을 만들다 'make memories', built with 만들다, not 하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 추억 for ordinary remembering — 'Do you remember his name?' must use 기억 (그 사람 이름 기억나요?), because 추억 implies sentiment and a whole experience, not mere recall.

usage: 감정이 상하다 'feelings spoil' is the fixed idiom for being hurt/offended
표현하다 'express' is the natural partner verb
숨기다 'hide/conceal' is the common opposite collocation
감정 + 의 + noun links the feeling to its shift
examples: 감정이 상했어요
My feelings got hurt
감정이 상하다 is THE set phrase for feeling hurt or offended
저는 감정 표현을 잘 안 해요
I don't really express my emotions
감정 표현 'emotional expression' is a common compound noun
이성보다 감정이 앞설 때가 있어요
There are times feeling runs ahead of reason
감정 vs 이성 'reason' is the classic paired contrast
nuance: 감정 is the Sino-Korean cover term for 'emotion/feeling', 감정 感情 — 感 'feel, sense' + 情 'feeling, affection' — the umbrella under which 기쁨, 슬픔, 분노 and the rest all sit, broader than any single mood. Two contrasts matter. Against 기분 (氣分), 'mood/how you feel right now': 기분 is the transient, surface state of the moment — 기분이 좋아요 'I'm in a good mood', 기분 나빠 'that bugs me' — and it is what you use in everyday chat, whereas 감정 is the deeper, more general category of human emotion and sounds more analytical. Against 이성 (理性), 'reason/rationality': 감정 vs 이성 is the standard 'heart vs head' pairing in Korean. The signature idiom is 감정이 상하다, literally 'the feelings spoil', meaning to get hurt or offended — a phrase learners must know. The English-speaker pitfall: for everyday 'I feel good/bad' do not say 감정이 좋아요; the natural sentence is 기분이 좋아요. Reserve 감정 for talking about emotions in general, expressing/hiding them (감정을 표현하다/숨기다), or being hurt (감정이 상하다).
